Local or temporary currents are produced by winds, the discharge of rivers, the fusion of fields of ice, the evaporation of inland seas, and other causes. But, exclusive of these, which we shall not attempt to describe, there are certain permanent and general currents, which we supposed all to originate in two great movements--that of the tropical waters westward is ascribed to the agency of the trade winds, which blowing constantly in one direction, must impress their own motion on the sea to a certain extent. But the resulting current is necessarily modified by the position of the great continents. The motion of the polar waters towards the equator is not as well accounted for, nor perhaps as its general existence as well ascensioned. It is supposed, that the opaque separation of the equator, reducing the level of the sea there, the more elevated waters of the polar regions flow in to apply the loss; and, further, that the fusion of ice in these seas must produce an accumulation of water, while naturally seeks a level by moving to the equator.
